incidents.cause: The pilot's inability to maintain yaw control while transitioning to an out of ground effect hover due to a loss of tail rotor effectiveness.
The pilot's failure to compensate for the excessive rate of descent on final approach.  A contributing factor was the reported down draft.

The pilot’s failure to maintain adequate clearance from terrain while maneuvering the helicopter at a low altitude after departure. Contributing to the accident were the pilot’s distraction by the smoke in the cabin and the limited visible features in the snow-covered field to discern the helicopter
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll.
The total loss of engine power due to an insufficient fastener preload that led to the failure of the No. 2 connecting rod assembly.
The pilot not maintaining airspeed while performing an aerial application maneuver and the inadvertent stall he encountered.   Contributing to the accident was the gust of wind during the maneuver.

The pilot’s failure to maintain adequate airspeed while in a turn during initial climb and the exceedance of the airplane’s critical angle of attack, which resulted in an aerodynamic stall at a low altitude.
The pilot's incorrect action to continue the takeoff when he failed to maintain directional control during the takeoff roll.
The pilot's decision to attempt to takeoff in crosswind conditions that exceeded the airplane’s demonstrated crosswind capability.
The pilot's loss of directional control to the right for reasons that could not be determined during examination of the right main landing gear wheel and brake drum.

The loss of engine power during takeoff for reasons that could not be determined because postaccident examination of the airframe and engine did not reveal any anomalies that would have precluded normal operation.
The pilot's inadequate evaluation of the wind conditions at takeoff and failure to maintain an adequate airspeed, which resulted in a stall and collision with terrain during the initial climb.
The pilot did not maintain directional control of the airplane in gusting wind conditions.

The in-flight fracture of a stainless steel bolt that was used to secure the upper and lower wing cables to the outer attach point at the leading edge spar of the right wing due to stress corrosion cracking, which caused the right wing to fail and precluded controlled flight. The pilot's failure to open the fuel shutoff valve during the preflight examination of the airplane which resulted in a total loss of engine power during initial climb after takeoff due to fuel starvation.
The pilot's failure to maintain sufficient airspeed to prevent an inadvertent aerodynamic stall, and impact with terrain.
The pilot's failure to maintain control of the airplane during climbout. Contributing to the accident was the pilot’s lack of experience in the make and model of the airplane.
The pilot's delayed decision to abort the takeoff, which resulted in a collision with terrain.

The pilot's decision to continue the takeoff with reduced engine power, which resulted in a collision with terrain during the takeoff initial climb. Contributing to the accident was the partial loss of engine power for reasons that could not be determined because postaccident examination of the airf
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during the landing rollout in crosswind conditions, which resulted in a runway excursion and impact with equipment.
The pilot's inadequate flare, which resulted in a nose-low impact with glassy water and a subsequent nose-over. Contributing to the accident was the pilot's diverted attention while landing.
The pilot's improper landing flare that resulted in a hard landing and subsequent separation of the airplane's sponson.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during landing due to an encounter with sun glare.
The pilot’s failure to abort the takeoff roll when the engine did not produce full power.
The pilot’s premature retraction of the landing gear during a go-around, which resulted in a gear up landing.
A partial loss of engine power due to inadequate ignition from cracked spark plugs and a failed magneto.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during a water landing.
Failure of the left main landing gear to fully extend and lock for undetermined reasons as a functional test of the landing gear system could not duplicate the anomaly.
The loss of engine power during landing for undetermined reasons.
The pilot's continued visual flight into instrument meteorological conditions, which resulted in spatial disorientation and a loss of control.
The pilot's improper decision to depart from a runway not suitable for takeoff, which resulted in a loss of aircraft control.
A loss of engine power during cruise flight due to carburetor icing and the pilot's failure to apply carburetor heat, which resulted in a forced landing on rough/uneven terrain.
The pilot overcorrected when the airplane experienced a downdraft during the takeoff which resulted in the airplane stalling and impacting the terrain.
The pilot's improper landing flare and inadequate recovery from a bounced landing.
The pilot’s improper decision to fly into an area of unsuitable terrain which the airplane was unable to exit, resulting in an aerodynamic stall and subsequent impact with terrain.
A loss of airplane control on final approach for reasons that could not be determined.

The non-instrument-rated pilot's improper decision to initiate a visual flight rules flight into an area with low ceilings due to mountain obscuration, which resulted in controlled flight into terrain.
The private pilot’s inadequate preflight planning and fuel management and the flight instructor’s inadequate supervision, which resulted in a total loss of engine power due to fuel starvation.
The pilot's improper decision to continue a high approach with a tailwind, rather than perform a go-around, which resulted in an overrun on a wet, down-sloping, grassy runway.
The unoccupied airplanes exceedance of the critical angle of attack which resulted in a stall, subsequent inverted spin, and impact with terrain.

The failure of the airplane owner and maintenance personnel to follow the propeller manufacturer's recommend overhaul schedule, which resulted in a fatigue fracture of the propeller blade actuating pin and a loss of thrust in flight.
The pilot’s failure to maintain control of the airplane while landing with a gusting wind.
The paraglider pilot's failure to see and avoid the hot air balloon, which resulted in a midair collision.
The balloon pilot's encounter with higher-than-expected wind velocity, which resulted in a hard landing and passenger injury.
The pilot’s failure to maintain control of the balloon due to an unexpected high surface wind and downdraft, which resulted in a hard landing.
